title: Sickle cell disease
covers: The sickle mutation and genotypes, the acute and chronic complications (infection, splenic sequestration, pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke), screening and diagnosis, and treatment: hydroxyurea, transfusion, transplant, gene therapy and the newer drugs.

items.p: An inherited disorder with chronic hemolytic anemia, vaso-occlusive crises, organ damage and a shortened life. About 8 million people are affected, mostly where malaria is endemic.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive: two sickle genes, or one sickle gene and one thalassemia gene.
High HbF and coinherited α-thalassemia make the disease milder.
A point mutation puts valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain. HbS forms polymers when it loses oxygen, and the red cell sickles.

ul: Hemolysis gives anemia and fatigue
Vaso-occlusion gives pain and organ damage
Around both: inflammation, endothelial dysfunction and a tendency to clot

items.p: Lecturer's note: it is a systemic disease. Complications start in childhood and last for life: stroke, retinopathy, hearing loss, acute chest syndrome, pulmonary hypertension, gallstones, kidney damage, avascular necrosis and priapism (a painful sustained erection).

summary.h: Infection and a sudden drop in hemoglobin

items.p: The spleen stops working in early childhood. Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus, meningococcus) and Salmonella can kill within hours. Penicillin, vaccines, newborn diagnosis and family education cut deaths.

Acute splenic sequestration is a sudden enlargement of the spleen with a hemoglobin fall of 2 g/dL or more. It can cause shock and death and recurs in up to 67%. The lecturer noted that infections trigger it. Parents are taught to feel the spleen.

table: Red cells trapped in the spleen
Parvovirus B19 stops red cell production
Donor and own cells destroyed after transfusion
Careful small-volume transfusion; splenectomy if recurrent
Transfusion; keep away from pregnant contacts

items.p: Small volumes are used in sequestration because the trapped cells return to the circulation.

Dactylitis is painful swelling of the hands and feet from vaso-occlusion of the small bones. It is often the first complication, peaks between 6 months and 2 years, and is usually bilateral (lecturer's note). Early dactylitis may signal a more severe course.
Pain is the most common complication and the top reason children with SCD use health care (not the top cause of death).

ul: Triggers: cold, stress, illness, dehydration, high altitude
Acute pain: severe, needs an unplanned visit. Chronic pain: on most days for 6 months.
Acute pain is an emergency: first analgesic within 1 hour, reassess every 30–60 minutes
Opioids titrated to effect; NSAIDs for 5–7 days; low-dose ketamine if opioids fail
Use incentive spirometry throughout to prevent acute chest syndrome

items.p: A new lung infiltrate plus chest pain, fever, fast breathing, wheeze, cough or low oxygen. It can come with a pain crisis or on its own.
It is the second cause of hospital admission and the leading cause of death in adults with SCD (mortality up to 9%).

ul: Treat with incentive spirometry, antibiotics, oxygen, careful analgesia and transfusion
Hydroxyurea reduces recurrence

items.p: Without screening, 11% of children with HbSS have a stroke by age 20, and more than half recur without treatment.

ul: Children: usually ischemic. Silent infarcts affect learning.
Adults: hemorrhagic stroke in young adults; ischemic stroke at 35–65 years
Transcranial Doppler every year from age 2 to 16 in HbSS and HbSβ⁰
At least one MRI without sedation at early school age
Velocity of 200 cm/s or more: regular transfusions cut the stroke risk by age 18 from 11% to 1.9% (STOP trial)

items.note: The handwritten note on slide 15 says the Doppler measures "cerebral artery diameter". The test measures blood flow velocity (cm/s), as on slide 16. The note "treat: ↑Hb and ↓HbSC" most likely means lowering sickle hemoglobin (HbS); HbSC is a separate genotype. Worth checking with the lecturer.

ul: Anemia is normocytic in HbSS and microcytic in HbS/β-thalassemia
Smear: sickle cells, target cells, Howell–Jolly bodies (the spleen is not working), nucleated red cells
Electrophoresis or HPLC: high HbS, often raised HbF; high HbA2 in HbS/β-thalassemia

table: Penicillin; full vaccines including pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, flu
Stop penicillin if no splenectomy and no invasive pneumococcal infection

items.p: Today 93.9% of children with HbSS or HbSβ⁰ reach age 18. The move from pediatric to adult care is a high-risk period.
Hydroxyurea is the backbone. It raises HbF, lowers white cells and improves red cell hydration. It is safe from 9 months of age.

ul: Start early and give the maximum tolerated dose
It cuts pain crises, acute chest syndrome, admissions, transfusions and Doppler velocities
Stop it before pregnancy
REACH (2024): escalating to 20–35 mg/kg/day beat a fixed 17.5 mg/kg/day, with 79% less acute chest syndrome and no extra toxicity

table: Acute chest syndrome, sudden fall in hemoglobin, before major surgery, selected pregnancies
Stroke or abnormal Doppler, multi-organ failure, complications despite hydroxyurea

items.p: Lecturer's note: for regular transfusion, use exchange transfusion if possible. Match Rh (C, E) and K antigens to prevent alloimmunization. Watch for iron overload and hyperhemolysis. Minor surgery needs no transfusion.
Stem cell transplant is the established cure: about 95% with a matched sibling, best done young and before organ damage.

items.note: Slide 25 says about 1 in 3 patients has a matched sibling donor. Most sources give a lower figure (under 20%). Not tested in the questions.

items.p: Gene therapy (FDA, December 2023, age 12 and over) uses the patient's own stem cells, so no donor and no graft-versus-host disease. Busulfan is still needed.

table: CRISPR cuts the BCL11A switch; fetal hemoglobin turns back on
97% free of pain crises for 12 months
A viral vector adds a new β-globin gene

items.p: Newer drugs have disappointed: L-glutamine has a modest effect, crizanlizumab lost its EU approval, voxelotor was withdrawn worldwide, mitapivat gave mixed results. Lecturer's note: hydroxyurea is best.

ul: 387 patients, clustered in the North (42.5%) and South (28.4%); high consanguinity; gene influx from neighboring countries
Newborn screening of 10,095 babies: 2.1% had an abnormal hemoglobin (3.5% in the North); HbS was 81% of them, HbD 12%
Prevention: awareness, carrier screening in high school, premarital testing, prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis

cards.a: Point mutation: valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain
When deoxygenated (it stays a monomer when oxygenated)

cards.q: SCD genotypes from most to least severe
cards.a: HbSS and S/β⁰-thalassemia (severe); HbSC or HbSD (less severe); S/β⁺-thalassemia (mild to moderate)

cards.q: Two factors that reduce SCD severity
cards.a: High HbF and coinherited α-thalassemia

cards.q: Why are young children with SCD at risk of fatal infection, and from what?
cards.a: Loss of splenic function; encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus, meningococcus) and Salmonella
Sudden splenic enlargement with a hemoglobin fall of 2 g/dL or more

cards.q: Three causes of a sudden drop in hemoglobin in SCD
cards.a: Acute splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), hyperhemolysis

cards.q: Sequestration versus aplastic crisis: spleen and reticulocytes
cards.a: Sequestration: large spleen, high reticulocytes. Aplastic crisis: spleen unchanged, reticulocytes very low.
Urgent, careful small-volume transfusion (trapped cells return to the circulation); splenectomy if recurrent

cards.q: Hyperhemolysis: what it is and treatment
cards.a: Destruction of donor and own red cells after transfusion; avoid more transfusion, give steroids and IVIG
Painful swelling of hands and feet from vaso-occlusion; often the first complication; peak 6 months to 2 years; usually bilateral
Cold, stress, illness, dehydration, high altitude

cards.q: Acute pain in SCD: timing targets (ASH 2020)
cards.a: First analgesic within 1 hour; reassess and re-dose every 30–60 minutes
New pulmonary infiltrate plus chest pain, fever, tachypnea, wheezing, cough or hypoxia
2nd cause of hospitalization; leading cause of death in adults with SCD

cards.q: Stroke in SCD: children versus adults
cards.a: Children: usually ischemic. Young adults: hemorrhagic. Age 35–65: ischemic.
Yearly from age 2 to 16 in HbSS and HbSβ⁰; abnormal at 200 cm/s or more

cards.q: What is done for an abnormal transcranial Doppler?
cards.a: Regular transfusions: stroke risk by age 18 falls from 11% to 1.9% (STOP)
Sickle cells, target cells, Howell–Jolly bodies, nucleated red cells

cards.q: HbSS versus HbS/β-thalassemia: MCV and HbA2
cards.a: HbSS: normocytic. HbS/β-thalassemia: microcytic with high HbA2.

cards.q: Penicillin prophylaxis in SCD: start and stop
cards.a: Start by 2 months; stop at age 5 if no splenectomy and no invasive pneumococcal infection
Raises HbF; lowers white cells; improves red cell hydration
Start early (safe from 9 months) and escalate to the maximum tolerated dose; stop before pregnancy
Acute chest syndrome, sudden fall in hemoglobin, before major surgery, selected pregnancies
Stroke or abnormal transcranial Doppler, multi-organ failure, complications despite hydroxyurea

cards.q: Antigens matched to prevent alloimmunization in SCD
cards.a: Rh (C, E) and K
Exa-cel: CRISPR cuts BCL11A so HbF turns back on. Lovo-cel: viral vector adds a β-globin gene (boxed warning for blood cancer).
Patient's own cells: no donor, no graft-versus-host disease; still needs myeloablative busulfan

cards.q: Where does SCD cluster in Lebanon?
cards.a: North and South Lebanon (high consanguinity, gene influx from neighboring countries)

questions.stem: Sickle cell disease needs two defective genes. Besides two sickle genes, which combination does the inheritance slide name?

questions.explanation: HbSS and S/β⁰-thalassemia are severe; HbSC and HbSD are generally less severe; S/β⁺-thalassemia is mild to moderate. A: HbSC is generally less severe. C: That is S/β⁺-thalassemia. D: That is sickle trait. E: HbSD is generally less severe.

questions.explanation: HbS: a point mutation puts valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain. HbS polymerizes when deoxygenated. A: Not HbS. C: Not HbS. D: Not HbS. E: Not HbS.

options.B: Oxygenated conditions, where monomers form polymers
options.C: Deoxygenated conditions, where polymers break into monomers
options.D: Alkaline conditions, where tetramers lose their heme
options.E: Iron-deficient conditions, where chains fail to pair

questions.explanation: HbS is a monomer in oxygenated conditions and polymerizes in deoxygenated conditions, sickling the red cell. B: Oxygenated HbS stays a monomer. C: Deoxygenation drives polymer formation. D: Not the mechanism shown. E: Not the mechanism shown.

questions.explanation: Six pillars: comprehensive care, pain management, hydroxyurea, transfusion, cure (transplant, gene therapy), new drugs. Foundation: newborn screening, family education and a medical home. A: Not the foundation shown. B: Hydroxyurea is a pillar. C: These are pillars. D: New drugs are a pillar.

questions.stem: Each is a warning sign the team teaches families EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Warning signs: fever, pallor, big spleen, chest pain, weakness. B: Taught. C: Taught. D: Taught. E: Taught.

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have HbSS on the heel-prick test. When should penicillin prophylaxis start?
questions.explanation: Birth: heel-prick test (HPLC). By 2 months: penicillin and full vaccines. Age 2: yearly TCD. Age 5: stop penicillin if criteria are met. A: By 2 months. B: By 2 months. D: Age 2 is when TCD starts. E: Prophylaxis starts by 2 months.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old with HbSS has an intact spleen and has never had invasive pneumococcal infection. What is done with his penicillin?
questions.explanation: Stop penicillin at age 5 if there was no splenectomy and no invasive pneumococcal infection. A: Stop at 5. B: Stop at 5. C: Stop at 5. D: Stop at 5.

questions.stem: What does the survival curve on the newborn screening slide show?

options.A: Children with HbSS diagnosed at birth survive the same as those diagnosed later
options.B: Children with HbSS diagnosed at birth survive better than those diagnosed later
options.C: Children with HbSC diagnosed at birth survive worse than those diagnosed later
options.D: Children given hydroxyurea survive better than those given penicillin
options.E: Children screened by TCD survive better than those screened by MRI

questions.explanation: Newborn screening and early prevention save lives: survival was higher in children diagnosed at birth. A: The curves separate. C: The curve is for HbSS, and survival is better. D: Not what the curve compares. E: Not what the curve compares.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with SCD arrives at the emergency department with severe back pain. What is the target time for the first analgesic dose?
questions.explanation: ASH 2020: rapid triage, treat as an emergency; first analgesic within 1 hour; reassess and re-dose every 30–60 minutes; watch for ACS. A: Within 1 hour. B: Treat as an emergency. C: Within 1 hour. E: Treat first.

questions.stem: Which use of the pain toolbox matches ASH 2020?

options.A: Low-dose ketamine as the first drug before opioids
options.B: NSAIDs as a long course of 5–7 weeks
options.C: Low-dose ketamine for pain not controlled by opioids
options.D: Opioids at a fixed dose for each patient
options.E: Massage and relaxation in place of analgesics

questions.explanation: Opioids titrated to effect by an individualized plan; NSAIDs short course, 5–7 days; low-dose ketamine for pain not controlled by opioids; non-drug measures (massage, relaxation, virtual reality). A: It follows opioid failure. B: A short course of 5–7 days. D: Titrated to effect by an individualized plan. E: Non-drug measures are added, not substituted.

questions.stem: How long is the NSAID course in the acute pain toolbox?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs: short course, 5–7 days. B: Shorter than stated. C: Longer than stated. D: Days, not weeks. E: Far too long.

questions.stem: Which statement about hydroxyurea's approval is correct?

options.A: First FDA-approved drug for SCD: adults 2017, children 2019
options.B: Second FDA-approved drug for SCD: adults 1998, children 2017
options.C: First FDA-approved drug for SCD: adults 1986, children 1998
options.D: First FDA-approved drug for SCD: adults 1998, children 2023
options.E: First FDA-approved drug for SCD: adults 1998, children 2017

questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea was the first FDA-approved drug for SCD (adults 1998, children 2017). A: 1998 and 2017. B: It was the first. C: Those are the penicillin and TCD milestones. D: 2023 is gene therapy.

questions.stem: What is the main beneficial action of hydroxyurea in SCD?
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea raises HbF; it also lowers white cells and improves red cell hydration. A: Voxelotor. C: Crizanlizumab. D: L-glutamine. E: Mitapivat.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old with HbSS is started on hydroxyurea. How should it be dosed?

options.B: At half the usual adult dose

questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea is safe from 9 months; give the maximum tolerated dose (REACH: 20–35 mg/kg/day beat a fixed 17.5). A: Escalation beat this (REACH). B: Not the advice. C: Not the advice. E: It is given continuously.

questions.stem: Each is reduced by hydroxyurea according to the lecture EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea cuts pain crises, ACS, hospitalizations, transfusions and TCD velocities; it raises HbF. A: Reduced. C: Reduced. D: Reduced. E: Reduced.

questions.stem: Which gaps in hydroxyurea use does the lecture list?

options.A: Over-prescribed and over-dosed; myelosuppression; reluctance to stop
options.B: Under-prescribed and under-dosed; kidney failure; high cost
options.C: Unsafe in infants; myelosuppression; loss of effect after a year
options.D: Under-prescribed; boxed warning for blood cancer; infertility
options.E: Under-prescribed and under-dosed; myelosuppression; reluctance to use

questions.explanation: Gaps: under-prescribed, often under-dosed; myelosuppression; reluctance to use. A: Under-prescribed and under-dosed. B: Myelosuppression and reluctance. C: Safe from 9 months. D: The boxed warning is lovo-cel's.

questions.stem: Each is an indication for a single (episodic) transfusion in SCD EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Single (episodic): acute chest syndrome, sudden fall in Hb, before major surgery, selected pregnancies. Transfusion is not needed for minor surgery. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which patient needs chronic (regular) transfusion?

options.B: An adult with a first acute chest syndrome
options.C: A child with a first splenic sequestration
options.D: A child with a previous stroke
options.E: A woman in an uncomplicated pregnancy

questions.explanation: Chronic transfusion: stroke or abnormal TCD, multi-organ failure, complications despite hydroxyurea (exchange transfusion if possible). A: No transfusion needed. B: Single (episodic) transfusion. C: Careful single transfusion. E: Selected pregnancies, single.

questions.stem: What did the lecturer write beside "chronic (regular)" transfusion?

options.A: Give simple transfusion in small volumes

questions.explanation: The note beside chronic transfusion: give exchange transfusion if possible. A: That is splenic sequestration. B: Not the note. D: The thalassemia schedule. E: Not the note.

questions.stem: How is alloimmunization prevented in transfused patients with SCD (ASH 2020)?

options.A: Match Rh (C, E) and K antigens
options.C: Match HLA class I and II antigens

questions.explanation: Alloimmunization: match Rh (C, E) and K antigens. Other risks: delayed hemolytic reactions, hyperhemolysis, and iron overload (monitor and chelate). B: Rh C, E and K. C: That is transplant matching. D: Not the safeguard named. E: That treats hyperhemolysis.

questions.stem: What cure rate is given for stem cell transplant from a matched sibling in SCD?
questions.explanation: Stem cell transplant is the established cure; an HLA-matched sibling is the best donor, with about 95% cure. A: The exa-cel pain-free figure. B: The sequestration recurrence figure. C: Too low. D: Too low.

questions.stem: Who is a transplant candidate under ASH 2021?

options.A: Severe disease (stroke, recurrent pain or ACS), adult, after organ damage
options.B: Mild disease (HbSC without crises), young, before organ damage
options.C: Any patient with a matched sibling, whatever the severity
options.D: Severe disease (stroke, recurrent pain or ACS), young, before organ damage
options.E: Severe disease, once gene therapy and hydroxyurea have both failed

questions.explanation: ASH 2021: severe disease (stroke, recurrent pain or ACS, alloimmunization); young, before organ damage. Risks: GVHD, infertility, infection; cost. A: Young, before organ damage. B: Severe disease. C: Selected for severe disease. E: Not the criterion.

questions.stem: Which order of steps describes gene therapy?

options.A: Give busulfan, collect CD34+ cells, modify them, reinfuse
options.B: Collect CD34+ cells, modify them, give busulfan, reinfuse
options.C: Collect CD34+ cells, give busulfan, reinfuse, modify them
options.D: Collect donor cells, modify them, give busulfan, reinfuse
options.E: Collect CD34+ cells, modify them, reinfuse, give busulfan

questions.explanation: 1 Collect the patient's own CD34+ stem cells. 2 Modify: add a working gene (lentiviral vector) or edit DNA (CRISPR). 3 Condition with myeloablative busulfan. 4 Reinfuse. A: Cells are collected before conditioning. C: Modification is done in the lab before reinfusion. D: The cells are the patient's own. E: Conditioning comes before reinfusion.

questions.stem: Which statement about gene therapy for SCD is correct?

options.A: It needs an HLA-matched sibling donor
options.B: It carries a risk of GVHD

questions.explanation: Gene therapy: collect the patient's own CD34+ cells, modify them, give myeloablative busulfan, reinfuse. No donor, no GVHD, but still myeloablation. A: The patient's own cells are used. B: No donor, no GVHD. D: Myeloablative busulfan is needed. E: Age 12 or older.

questions.stem: Exa-cel (Casgevy) cuts the BCL11A switch. What is the result?

options.B: A new β-globin gene is added

questions.explanation: Exa-cel: CRISPR cuts BCL11A, which silences fetal Hb; HbF turns back on and blocks sickling; 97% free of pain crises for ≥ 12 months. B: Lovo-cel. C: Crizanlizumab. D: Voxelotor. E: Mitapivat.

questions.stem: What outcome was reported for exa-cel in SCD?

options.B: 79% free of acute chest syndrome for at least 12 months
options.C: 95% cured with a matched sibling donor
options.D: 97% free of pain crises for at least 12 months
options.E: 67% free of pain crises for at least 24 months

questions.explanation: 97% were free of pain crises for ≥ 12 months (29 of 30). A: The SCD outcome is freedom from pain crises. B: A REACH figure. C: The transplant figure. E: 97%, 12 months.

questions.stem: Which statement about Lovo-cel (Lyfgenia) is correct?

options.A: Gene addition by viral vector; boxed warning for liver failure
options.B: Gene addition by viral vector; boxed warning for blood cancer
options.C: CRISPR gene editing; boxed warning for blood cancer
options.D: Gene addition by viral vector; approved from age 2
options.E: CRISPR gene editing; approved without conditioning

questions.explanation: Lovo-cel: gene addition with a viral vector carrying a new β-globin gene; boxed warning for blood cancer risk. A: Blood cancer. C: It is gene addition. D: Age 12 or older. E: Gene addition, with busulfan.

questions.stem: Each applies to both SCD gene therapies approved in December 2023 EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Both: age ≥ 12 with vaso-occlusive events; busulfan, infertility risk, high cost, 15-year follow-up. A: Applies to both. B: Applies to both. C: Applies to both. D: Applies to both.

questions.stem: What does the timeline say about L-glutamine?

options.A: Approved in 2017; inhibits HbS polymerization; large effect
options.B: Approved in 2019; blocks cell adhesion; modest effect
options.C: Approved in 2017; reduces oxidative stress; modest effect
options.D: Withdrawn in 2024; reduces oxidative stress; excess deaths
options.E: Approved in 2025; activates pyruvate kinase; mixed effect

questions.explanation: 2017: L-glutamine approved (FDA); reduces oxidative stress; modest effect. A: Oxidative stress; modest. B: That is crizanlizumab. D: That is voxelotor. E: That is mitapivat.

questions.stem: Which pairing of the two drugs approved in 2019 with their mechanisms is correct?

options.A: Crizanlizumab: HbS polymerization inhibitor; voxelotor: anti-adhesion antibody
options.B: Crizanlizumab: anti-adhesion antibody; voxelotor: pyruvate kinase activator
options.C: Crizanlizumab: fetal hemoglobin inducer; voxelotor: HbS polymerization inhibitor
options.D: Crizanlizumab: anti-adhesion antibody; voxelotor: HbS polymerization inhibitor
options.E: Crizanlizumab: anti-adhesion antibody; voxelotor: oxidative stress reducer

questions.explanation: 2019: crizanlizumab (anti-adhesion antibody) and voxelotor (HbS polymerization inhibitor) approved by the FDA. A: Reversed. B: That is mitapivat. C: An anti-adhesion antibody. E: That is L-glutamine.

questions.stem: What later happened to crizanlizumab and voxelotor?

options.A: Voxelotor lost EU approval after STAND; crizanlizumab was withdrawn worldwide
options.B: Crizanlizumab lost EU approval after RISE UP; voxelotor gained pediatric approval
options.C: Both stayed approved after confirmatory trials showed fewer crises
options.D: Crizanlizumab was withdrawn for excess deaths; voxelotor failed in STAND
options.E: Crizanlizumab lost EU approval after STAND; voxelotor was withdrawn worldwide

questions.explanation: 2023: crizanlizumab EU approval revoked (STAND: no benefit over placebo). 2024: voxelotor withdrawn worldwide (deaths and more crises in later data). A: Reversed. B: STAND; voxelotor was withdrawn. C: Neither held up. D: Reversed reasons.

questions.stem: What lesson does the lecture draw from the new-drug timeline, including the RISE UP result for mitapivat?

options.A: Approval based on clinical outcomes must be confirmed by lab endpoints
options.B: Drugs that raise hemoglobin reliably reduce pain crises
options.C: Approval based on lab endpoints must be confirmed by clinical outcomes
options.D: New drugs should replace hydroxyurea as the backbone

questions.explanation: Mitapivat 2025: mixed results (RISE UP: Hb improved; other endpoints mixed). Lesson: approval based on lab endpoints must be confirmed by clinical outcomes. The handwritten note: hydroxyurea is best. A: Reversed. B: RISE UP raised Hb with mixed other endpoints. D: The lecturer wrote that hydroxyurea is best. E: Not the lesson.

questions.stem: What share of children reach age 18 today, by genotype?

options.A: 93.9% with HbSS or HbSβ⁰; 98.4% with HbSC or HbSβ⁺
options.B: 98.4% with HbSS or HbSβ⁰; 93.9% with HbSC or HbSβ⁺
options.C: 93.9% with HbSS or HbSβ⁺; 98.4% with HbSC or HbSβ⁰
options.D: 50–80% with HbSS or HbSβ⁰; 98.4% with HbSC or HbSβ⁺
options.E: 67% with HbSS or HbSβ⁰; 95% with HbSC or HbSβ⁺

questions.explanation: 93.9% reach age 18 with HbSS or HbSβ⁰; 98.4% with HbSC or HbSβ⁺. B: Reversed; the severe genotypes do worse. C: β⁰ groups with HbSS. D: 50–80% is early mortality in low-resource countries. E: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: Which milestone is matched with its year?
questions.explanation: 1986 penicillin prophylaxis; 1998 TCD screening (STOP); 2006 universal newborn screening (US); 2017 hydroxyurea for children; 2023 gene therapy. A: 1998 is TCD screening (STOP). C: 2006 is universal newborn screening in the US. D: 2017 is hydroxyurea for children. E: 2023 is gene therapy.

questions.stem: As childhood survival improves, which period does the lecture call high-risk?

options.A: The move from pediatric to adult care
options.B: The first 6 months of life, while HbF is high

questions.explanation: Deaths are shifting to adults: the move from pediatric to adult care is a high-risk period. B: HbF still protects then. C: Not the period named. D: Not the period named. E: Not the period named.

questions.stem: When is carrier screening ideally done, according to the prevention slide?

options.A: At birth, with the heel-prick test
options.B: In high school, with genetic counseling
options.C: At age 2, with the first TCD

questions.explanation: Carrier screening: ideally in high school, with genetic counseling; premarital testing; prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis for at-risk couples (25% risk in each pregnancy). A: That is newborn screening for disease. C: Not carrier screening. D: Earlier is the aim. E: Before marriage at the latest.

questions.stem: What does the Lebanese SCD series (n = 387) show?

options.A: Spread evenly across Lebanon; high consanguinity; gene influx from neighbors
options.B: Clustered in Beirut and Bekaa; low consanguinity; gene influx from neighbors
options.C: Clustered in North and South; high consanguinity; gene influx from neighbors
options.D: Clustered in North and South; low consanguinity; no outside origin
options.E: Clustered in Mount Lebanon; high consanguinity; gene influx from Africa

questions.explanation: n = 387: North 42.5%, South 28.4%. Key points: clustered in North and South Lebanon, high consanguinity, gene influx from neighboring countries. A: Even spread describes thalassemia. B: North and South; high consanguinity. D: High consanguinity and gene influx. E: North (42.5%) and South (28.4%).

questions.stem: What did newborn screening of 10,095 babies in Lebanese public hospitals find?

options.A: 2.1% with abnormal hemoglobin; HbC the commonest, then HbS
options.B: 21% with abnormal hemoglobin; HbS the commonest, then HbD
options.C: 3.5% with abnormal hemoglobin; HbD the commonest, then HbS
options.D: 0.2% with abnormal hemoglobin; HbS the commonest, then HbO-Arab
options.E: 2.1% with abnormal hemoglobin; HbS the commonest, then HbD

questions.explanation: 10,095 newborns screened; 211 with abnormal Hb; 2.1% incidence in Lebanon, 3.5% in the North. HbS 81%, HbD 12%, HbC 4%, HbO-Arab 3%. A: HbS 81%, HbD 12%, HbC 4%. B: 211 of 10,095 is 2.1%. C: 3.5% is the North; HbS leads. D: 2.1%; HbD is second.

questions.stem: What did the REACH trial (2024) compare in African children?

options.A: Hydroxyurea escalated to 20–35 mg/kg/day versus regular transfusion
options.B: Hydroxyurea at a fixed 17.5 mg/kg/day versus placebo
options.C: Hydroxyurea escalated to 50–70 mg/kg/day versus a fixed 35 mg/kg/day
options.D: Hydroxyurea escalated to 20–35 mg/kg/day versus a fixed 17.5 mg/kg/day
options.E: Hydroxyurea at a fixed 17.5 mg/kg/day versus L-glutamine

questions.explanation: REACH 2024: escalating to the maximum tolerated dose (20–35 mg/kg/day) beat a fixed 17.5 mg/kg/day dose. A: Both arms were hydroxyurea. B: Escalated versus fixed dose. C: 20–35 versus 17.5. E: Escalated versus fixed dose.

questions.stem: In REACH, which event fell the most at the maximum tolerated dose, and what happened to toxicity?

options.A: Acute chest syndrome, by 79%; dose-limiting toxicity did not increase
options.B: Acute chest syndrome, by 79%; dose-limiting toxicity doubled
options.C: Vaso-occlusive events, by 79%; dose-limiting toxicity did not increase
options.D: Malaria, by 79%; dose-limiting toxicity rose in malaria areas
options.E: Serious adverse events, by 40%; dose-limiting toxicity did not increase

questions.explanation: Reductions: acute chest syndrome 79%, serious adverse events 58%, non-malarial infections 48%, malaria 42%, vaso-occlusive events 40%. Dose-limiting toxicity did not increase; safe in malaria-endemic settings. B: Toxicity did not increase. C: Vaso-occlusive events fell by 40%. D: Malaria fell by 42%; it was safe there. E: Serious adverse events fell by 58%.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with SCD recovers from a second episode of sudden pallor with a large, tender spleen. Besides teaching the parents to feel the spleen, which step is considered?
questions.explanation: Recurrent acute splenic sequestration: teach parents, consider splenectomy, start or optimize hydroxyurea. A: Start or optimize it. B: Not indicated. C: Not indicated. D: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with HbSS suddenly develops right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Which stroke type is most likely at her age?
questions.explanation: Stroke in children with SCD is usually ischemic, a leading cause of morbidity and death; silent infarcts affect learning. Young adults: hemorrhagic. A: Most frequent in young adults. C: Not the stated pattern. D: Not the stated pattern. E: Not the stated pattern.
